kakekotoba.interaction: Functions as a proper place name (Tamukeyama, a mountain pass where travelers made offerings) while also transparently containing the verb 手向く ("to make an offering"), echoing the 幣 (nusa) offering just mentioned — the place name itself enacts the ritual act of offering.

jokotoba.text: このたびは幣もとりあへず手向山
jokotoba.function: Sets up the narrative situation — a hurried journey with no time to prepare formal offerings — building toward the resolution in the shimo-no-ku where the maple leaves themselves become the offering. Not a fixed epithet; freely composed for this journey scene, and longer than 5 morae, but tightly integrated with the poem's logic rather than merely a sonic bridge.

honkadori.source_poem: Poems referencing offerings (幣) at mountain passes such as Tamukeyama were a established travel-poem convention in Man'yōshū and early Heian poetry (e.g. traveler's offering poems at famous passes)

kigo.note: 紅葉 (autumn maple leaves) is one of the most canonical autumn images in waka, conventionally likened to brocade (錦) scattered on mountains — here explicitly compared to a nishiki brocade offered to the gods, making it the poem's dominant seasonal and visual image.

bipartite.kami_theme: The traveler, caught unprepared on this journey, has no time to properly prepare the ritual cloth/paper offerings (nusa) required at the sacred mountain pass of Tamukeyama.
bipartite.shimo_theme: The scattered autumn maple leaves, brilliant as brocade, are offered instead — let the gods do as they will with this natural, unplanned offering.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku establishes a ritual deficiency (no formal offering prepared), and the shimo-no-ku resolves it by revealing that nature itself — the maple-leaf brocade — has supplied the offering in place of human effort, transforming an apology into an act of devotional surrender ('as the gods will').

source_jp:
このたびは
幣もとりあへず
手向山
紅葉のにしき
神のまにまに
